subject: stocks
title: A Slice of a Company
summary: A share of stock makes you a part owner of a company. Here's how owners earn money, and how they can lose it.

keys.prompt: What do you own when you buy a share of stock?
keys.answer: A small piece of a company. Owning stock makes you a part owner.

cards.title: A stand that needs help
cards.text: Imagine your lemonade stand gets really popular. You want a second stand, but you don't have the money. What if your friends chipped in, and each one owned part of the stands? That is the big idea behind stocks.

cards.question: Stocks of big companies, as a group: how often have they lost money in a year?
cards.reveal: About one year out of every three, on average. Stock prices go down as well as up.

cards.title: A share is a slice
cards.text: A stock gives you a share of a company. That means you own a small piece of it. Lots of people can each own a piece. Stocks are also called equities.
cards.example: Say a pizza shop is split into 100 equal shares. If you own 5 shares, you own 5 of the 100 pieces.

cards.title: Why companies sell shares
cards.text: Companies sell stock to get money. They might use it to make new products or build new places. The people who buy the shares become part owners.

why.q: Why would a company sell pieces of itself?
why.a: It gets money now to grow, like launching new products or building something new.

cards.title: Two ways to earn
cards.text: Owners can earn money in two ways. The price of a share can go up, so you sell it for more than you paid. Or the company can pay owners part of its profit. That payment is called a dividend.
cards.example: Say you buy one share for $20. Later you sell it for $25. You earned $5.

cards.title: Prices go down too
cards.text: Stock prices can drop. A company might make a bad product, or big news might shake things up. Stocks of big companies, as a group, have lost money in about one year out of three. So you can lose money.

why.q: If stocks can lose money, why do people buy them?
why.a: People who kept their stocks for a long time, like 15 years, have mostly done well. But there is no promise.

cards.title: Don't own just one
cards.text: No one knows for sure which company will do well. So lots of people own many different stocks. Then one bad company doesn't sink everything.
cards.example: Say you own shares in 10 companies. If one has a bad year, you still own the other 9.

cards.question: If you could own a slice of any company, which one would you pick, and why?
nudges: Do lots of people buy what it makes?
What might make its price go down?

questions.q: What does owning a share of stock make you?

options.text: A part owner of the company
options.why: Yes! A share is a small piece of the company.
No. You don't work there. You own a small piece of it.

options.text: Someone the company owes a loan to
options.why: That's a different thing. A stock is a piece of ownership, not a loan.

questions.q: You buy a share for $20 and sell it for $25. How much did you earn?

options.why: You subtract what you paid. $25 minus $20 is $5.
$25 is what you sold it for. You paid $20, so you earned $5.

options.text: Part of the company's profit paid to owners
options.why: Yes! It's one of the two ways owners can earn.

options.text: The price you pay for one share
options.why: No. A dividend is profit the company pays out to its owners.

options.text: A fee for selling a stock
options.why: No. A dividend is money owners get, not money they pay.

sources.title: Stocks - FAQs
sources.supports: Stocks give stockholders a share of ownership in a company and are also called equities; companies issue stock to get money for things like launching new products or building new facilities; people earn when the price rises (capital appreciation) or from dividends; prices move down as well as up and you can lose money; prices are affected by things like a faulty product or political or market events; large company stocks as a group have lost money about one out of every three years; people who stuck with stocks for long periods, say 15 years, generally have been rewarded; owning a number of different stocks offsets some of the risk.

sources.title: Dividend
sources.supports: A dividend is a portion of a company's profit paid to shareholders.
